analysis.one_liner: Blocks drugmakers from delaying generic competition by switching patients to a tweaked version of the same drug.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee unanimously approved the bill in April 2025 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the Senate has not yet voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug's patents are about to expire, its maker sometimes pulls it off the market or stops making it and replaces it with a slightly altered, still-patented version — the same drug under a new label, so cheap copies never arrive. This bill defines that tactic as an unfair method of competition under the FTC Act. The Federal Trade Commission could stop a manufacturer mid-switch, and in court cases could force it to hand back profits or pay restitution to people overcharged during the switch. A manufacturer can defend itself by showing a safety, supply, or other genuine reason, and the FTC can still challenge conduct under existing antitrust law.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need drugs that are nearing the end of their patent life. If the bill works as written, cheaper generic and biosimilar versions reach the market on the original schedule instead of being delayed by a reformulated successor, which means lower out-of-pocket costs at the pharmacy. Insurers and government programs that pay drug bills also benefit from the lower prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients buying brand-name drugs near patent expiry

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes 'product hopping' — withdrawing or de-marketing a drug as a generic nears approval and selling a reformulated, still-patented follow-on instead — an unfair method of competition that the FTC can enforce [S2] [S3].

It creates a presumption that a manufacturer engaged in a prohibited 'hard switch' if, after learning a generic or biosimilar application was filed, it withdrew the original drug and sold a follow-on product [S2] [S3].
The FTC can sue in federal court to block a switch in progress and seek remedies including disgorgement of unjust profits and restitution to people harmed, with a five-year window [S3].

Manufacturers can escape liability only by showing they would have acted anyway and had a genuine safety, supply-disruption, or pro-competitive reason, and the FTC may still override that if the anticompetitive effects outweigh the benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers lose a major tool for extending monopoly pricing after their key patents expire. Some reformulation costs that a manufacturer can no longer recover through extended exclusivity could also fall back on it. Patients pay nothing new under the bill; they are on the receiving side of the lower prices it aims to produce.

drawbacks.text: The bill's main enforcement tool is the FTC, so its strength depends on which commission holds that the conduct is an 'unfair method of competition' — a moving target across administrations; a differently minded FTC could decline to bring cases [S3].

Defining when a reformulation 'impedes competition' and when a manufacturer has a 'legitimate pro-competitive reason' requires case-by-case judgments, and drugmakers argue that some changes are genuinely better medicines or safer products, raising the risk of legitimate improvements being chilled [S3].

The bill does nothing about the many other ways generic entry is delayed, such as settlement agreements that pay generics to stay off the market, so it targets one tactic rather than the whole problem [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs directly to patients in the form of earlier access to cheaper copies of expensive drugs, and the cost falls on the brand-name industry's ability to keep monopoly prices after patents lapse. The main honest caveat is enforcement risk: the law is only as strong as the FTC willing to use it, and its definitions will be tested in court. On balance, the bill targets a well-documented, specific delay tactic while leaving genuine safety and product improvements through the exclusion and justification provisions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee with an amendment in April 2025 and was placed on the Senate's calendar of business, where it sits awaiting a floor vote that the Senate has not yet scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Cornyn introduced the bill on March 13, 2025, with Senators Blumenthal, Grassley, and Durbin as original cosponsors, a bipartisan group [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment on April 3, 2025, and reported it on April 10 [S5].
The reported bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on April 10, 2025 (Calendar No. 43) [S3] [S5].
No further floor action has been recorded since the bill was placed on the calendar; Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drugmakers are better off so far: the tactic the bill bans remains fully usable while the bill waits on the Senate calendar without a scheduled vote.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill out of committee with an amendment on April 10, 2025

for.name: Sens. Richard Blumenthal and Dick Durbin
for.role: Democratic cosponsors on the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsors; supported the bill through committee

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed and lobbied against similar product-hopping bans, arguing legitimate reformulations would be swept in

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and chair, two Democratic cosponsors, and cleared the Judiciary Committee with an amendment favorably, with no recorded opposition votes.

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to withdraw a drug as its patent window closes and sell a still-patented reformulation instead, cutting off a core route to extended monopoly pricing. Patients bear that extended-pricing cost today, so the industry's interest runs against theirs.
Cheaper generics and biosimilars would reach the market on schedule instead of being displaced by reformulated successors; their gain in sales volume is the public's gain in lower prices.

analysis.trajectory: A bill reported out of committee and placed on the Senate calendar still needs a floor vote, which the majority leader can withhold indefinitely. Bills on patent-life and drug-pricing issues have previously moved as parts of larger packages; absent a negotiated spot on the floor schedule, this bill is likely to sit on the calendar through the end of 2026.
